questions.prompt: What is the difference between an Analogy and an Example?
questions.walkthrough: Both are specific cases used to illuminate a more general idea, but they work in opposite directions. An Example is a specific case that falls under a general idea: tomatoes are an example of fruit. An Analogy is a different specific case that resembles the case at hand in some general way: comparing a particle of radiation to a bullet shot from a gun lets you visualise one process through another. Examples sit inside the category; analogies sit alongside it. On the LSAT, illustrations are examples; analogies are cross-domain comparisons used to clarify.

questions.prompt: Which part of this answer refers to the Conclusion, which part refers to the Evidence?
questions.explanation: The directional word is "to support." Forward-pointing, so it points at the conclusion. Whatever follows "to support" is the conclusion (Y). Whatever sits before it is the evidence (X).

questions.prompt: Which part of this answer refers to the Conclusion, which part refers to the Evidence?
questions.phrase: appeals to X in order to Y
questions.explanation: "In order to" is forward-pointing, so whatever follows it is the conclusion (Y). The thing appealed to (X) is the evidence.

questions.prompt: Which part of this answer refers to the Conclusion, which part refers to the Evidence?
questions.phrase: infers that X on the grounds that Y
questions.explanation: "On the grounds that" is backward-pointing to evidence, so whatever follows it (Y) is the evidence. X is the inferred conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which part of this answer refers to the Conclusion, which part refers to the Evidence?
questions.explanation: "By" is backward-pointing to the tactic that accomplishes the move. Y is the specific tactic (evidence). X is the broader move being accomplished (conclusion).

questions.prompt: What is another name for a Supported Premise?
questions.walkthrough: Intermediate Conclusion (also called Subsidiary Conclusion). A Supported Premise functions as both a premise (it supports the main conclusion) and a sub-conclusion (it is supported by something else inside the argument). Two labels, same slot.

A claim is a statement being asserted. Typically a claim is a conclusion (the author asserts it as the point of the argument), but it can also be the conclusion attributed to an opposing view, or in some cases a premise being put forward for acceptance. The defining feature is the act of asserting, not the slot. If a sentence is putting a position on the table, it is a claim.

questions.prompt: Which part of this answer refers to the Conclusion, which part refers to the Evidence?
questions.phrase: concludes, from the claim that X, that Y
questions.explanation: "From" is backward-pointing to the starting claim, so X (the claim concluded from) is the evidence. Y is the conclusion drawn from it.

questions.prompt:
How are these terms related?

Explanation for a Phenomenon : Hypothesis
questions.walkthrough: They are the same kind of thing pitched at different confidence levels. A Phenomenon is the effect side of a cause-effect pair, the thing that needs explaining. An Explanation for that Phenomenon is the proposed cause. A Hypothesis is also a proposed cause, but the LSAT uses "hypothesis" specifically to flag a tentative or testable causal account. Every hypothesis on the LSAT is an explanation for some phenomenon. The hypothesis label adds the connotation of a guess waiting on evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a Counterexample and an Alternate Explanation?
questions.walkthrough: They attack different things. A Counterexample attacks a general claim by producing one specific case that does not fit it: if someone says all swans are white and you show them a black swan, that is a counterexample. An Alternate Explanation attacks a causal claim by proposing a different cause for the same effect: if someone says X caused Y and you say maybe Z caused Y instead, that is an alternate explanation. Counterexamples target generalisations. Alternate explanations target causal arguments.
